To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hypoxia-inducing factors (HIF), the mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOr) and the unfolded protein Response (UPR) are all involved in the control of the expression of angiogenic factors that have both vascular and immunological functions.

hypoxia-inducing factor 1α (HIF-1α) and the mechanistic target for rapamycin (MTOR) are key players in the regulation of angiogenic factors that are also involved in the generation of a hypoxic tumor micro-environment that favors immunotolerance.
hypoxia is a key driver of tumor progression and therapeutic resistance, and that targeting oxygen sensing may be a promising strategy to overcome these limitations.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the role of oxygen in the development of solid cancers, the role of hypoxia in the development of resistance to anti-cancer therapies and, finally, the role of HIF in the development of anti-cancer therapies.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of tumor angiogenesis in the context of cancer immunology, and developing novel therapeutic strategies to improve the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies.
the mechanisms that regulate hypoxia-driven angiogenesis, which in turn controls immunosuppression, and how this might be exploited to improve anti-cancer therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hypoxia is not a mere bystander, but a key driver of the tumor microenvironment that promotes angiogenesis and cancer immunotolerance and thus therapeutic failure.
hypoxia is a major player in cancer development and progression, and that hypoxia-induced angiogenesis plays a central role in the immunotolerance of solid cancers.
targeting angiogenesis in hypoxic cancer may have the potential to improve the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypoxic cancer cells use HIFs, UPR, and mTOR signaling to co-opt angiogenesis to create an immune suppressive tumor microenvironment.
hypoxia, by regulating angiogenesis, is a key driver of immunosuppression in the tumor micro-environment and a major cause of therapeutic failure.
the tumor microenvironment is a complex network that includes the tumor cells, the immune cells, the extracellular matrix (ECM) and the blood vessels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypoxia is an important regulator of both angiogenic and immunomodulating processes, which are tightly linked and should be targeted in parallel to improve the efficacy of anti-cancer therapies.
the tumor microenvironment, and the hypoxia-induced angiogenic factors that control it, can be targeted to enhance anti-cancer immunity.

targeting oxygen sensing might not only improve the efficacy of anti-angiogenic therapies, but also enhance immunotherapeutic strategies, including immune checkpoint blockade, which is currently the most promising approach to cancer immunotherapy.
